sections.title: Quoting & Job Profitability

questions.text: We've completed jobs that turned out to be less profitable than we expected when we quoted them.
Quotes depend heavily on one person's knowledge, experience or a spreadsheet only they really understand.
We don't consistently compare what a job actually cost against what we originally quoted.
questions.friction: Actual costs are not checked against quotes.

sections.opportunity: Connect quotes with actual job costs to see which work pays.

sections.title: Production & Scheduling

questions.text: We've committed to delivery dates without a clear view of whether we actually had the capacity to meet them.
questions.friction: Dates are promised without checking capacity.

questions.text: When priorities change, updating the production plan means manually changing several spreadsheets, documents or lists.
questions.friction: Schedule changes need several manual updates.

questions.text: If someone asks where a job is right now, finding the answer usually involves asking around or checking several places.
questions.friction: Job progress is hard to find.

sections.opportunity: Bring capacity, priorities and job progress into one clear production plan.

sections.title: Inventory & Purchasing

questions.text: Production has been delayed because material or components weren't available when they were needed.
Our stock records don't always match what's actually on the shelf.
questions.friction: Stock records do not match the shelf.

questions.text: We've bought material unnecessarily because we didn't have a reliable view of stock, demand or outstanding purchase orders.

sections.opportunity: Connect stock, demand and open purchase orders before buying.

sections.title: Information, Control & Growth

questions.text: The same information has to be manually copied, entered or updated in more than one spreadsheet, system or document.
questions.friction: Information is entered more than once.

questions.text: We've made a costly mistake because someone was working from the wrong information, an outdated version or a changed spreadsheet.
We're increasingly relying on specific people to remember how things work or where important information is kept.
questions.friction: Important knowledge sits with specific people.

sections.opportunity: Keep operational information in one shared, reliable place.

bands.title: Your spreadsheets still look like a workable fit.
bands.message: There’s no need to rush into ERP. Start with the issues you identified and check whether a simpler process can resolve them.

bands.title: You’re starting to outgrow your spreadsheets.
bands.message: Start with the areas at the top of the table. Work out where information gets lost or repeated, then explore whether a connected system could remove that work.

bands.title: Your spreadsheets may be making work harder than it needs to be.
bands.message: It’s worth reviewing how quoting, production and stock information fit together. Agree how those processes should work, then assess whether a connected manufacturing system would help.

nextQuestions: Do we understand how our most important processes should work?
Can we clearly explain how information should flow from quote through to delivery?
Are we willing to stop maintaining duplicate spreadsheets once information is managed properly elsewhere?
Do the people running the business broadly agree on how key processes should work?
Are we prepared to improve the process rather than simply reproduce every existing spreadsheet inside new software?
